Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Filmmaker Michael Moore, whose new documentary "Sicko" takes on America's health care system, faced off Tuesday with CNN chief medical correspondent and practicing neurosurgeon Dr. Sanjay Gupta. Michael Moore and CNN's Sanjay Gupta argued Tuesday about Gupta's report on Moore's film "Sicko" Moore criticized a report Gupta did on CNN Monday on "Sicko." "He said the facts were fudged," Moore said, referring to Gupta, on CNN's "Larry King Live." "That's a lie. None of the facts are fudged." Moore and Gupta shouted and argued over data Gupta used and data Moore used. Moore said his staffers backed up the film's facts to Gupta before the report aired and that Gupta aired it knowing his facts were wrong. Gupta disputed that.  Watch Moore, Gupta make their points » . "We try and look for some of the best sources we can possibly find," he said. "Michael has a lot of different numbers. ... You're sort of cherry-picking data from different reports." Both agreed, however, on the basic premise of "Sicko": Problems abound in America's health-care system and need to be fixed. "I thought it was a good movie, and I wanted to say that," Gupta said. "I think it strikes at the irrefutable fact -- it's broken. We get it." He praised Moore for raising awareness of the issue. However, Gupta said he was concerned that the movie -- which notes that other developed nations such as France and Canada have universal health care --suggests that health care in those countries is free. While patients may not pay for services at the doctor's office, they do pay high taxes to fund such a system, something Gupta said he was concerned that "Sicko" audiences might not realize. Moore responded by saying Americans pay more in copays, deductibles and insurance premiums. "We [America] have a system built on profit," the moviemaker said. He asked Gupta if the current system, which requires him to receive approval from an insurance company before performing some procedures, is cumbersome to him. "It's a shameful system, especially when I'm dealing with some of my patients," Gupta said. But he questioned Moore's apparent solution -- putting health care in the hands of the Bush administration, which Moore fiercely criticized in the past, particularly in his film "Fahrenheit 9/11." "The government actually used to do things right," Moore said in response. "The problem is who we put in power." Moore has adamantly opposed the war in Iraq and said the government should reprioritize -- a position he took many years before skepticism of the war's success abounded in Washington. "I am sorry we've taken so much time trying to correct [Gupta's] facts here tonight instead of talking about the real issue" -- the ailing health care system, Moore said. E-mail to a friend .

“We try to look for some of the best sources we can possibly find,” Gupta said. “Michael has a lot of different numbers. ... You’re sort of cherry-picking data from different reports.”

Both agreed, however, with the central premise of *Sicko*: America’s health care system is beset by problems that must be addressed.

“I thought it was a good movie, and I wanted to say that,” Gupta said. “I think it strikes at the irrefutable fact—it’s broken. We get it.” He also praised Moore for raising public awareness of the issue.

However, Gupta expressed concern that the film—which notes that other developed nations, including France and Canada, provide universal health care—suggests that health care in those countries is free. Although patients may not pay for services at the doctor’s office, they fund the system through high taxes, a point Gupta worried *Sicko* audiences might not recognize.

Moore responded that Americans pay more through copayments, deductibles and insurance premiums.

“We [America] have a system built on profit,” the filmmaker said. He asked Gupta whether the current system—which requires him to obtain approval from an insurance company before performing certain procedures—was cumbersome.

“It’s a shameful system, especially when I’m dealing with some of my patients,” Gupta said.

But Gupta questioned Moore’s apparent solution: placing health care in the hands of the Bush administration, which Moore had fiercely criticized in the past, particularly in his film *Fahrenheit 9/11*.

“The government actually used to do things right,” Moore replied. “The problem is who we put in power.”

Moore has adamantly opposed the war in Iraq and said the government should reorder its priorities—a position he took years before skepticism about the war’s success became widespread in Washington.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Michael Moore, the director behind the new documentary “Sicko,” debated CNN’s chief medical correspondent and practicing neurosurgeon, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, on Tuesday over the film’s examination of the U.S. health-care system.

The confrontation followed a CNN report about “Sicko” that Gupta presented Monday. Appearing on CNN’s “Larry King Live,” Moore objected to Gupta’s claim that the documentary had manipulated facts.

“He said the facts were fudged,” Moore said. “That’s a lie. None of the facts are fudged.”

The discussion became heated as the two men challenged each other’s statistics and raised their voices. Moore said members of his team had verified the film’s information for Gupta before the segment was broadcast. He also accused Gupta of airing the report despite knowing that his own figures were incorrect. Gupta denied that allegation.

“We try and look for some of the best sources we can possibly find,” Gupta said. He argued that Moore relied on numerous figures and was “sort of cherry-picking data from different reports.”

Despite their disagreement, both men accepted the central argument of “Sicko”: The American health-care system has widespread problems that must be addressed.

Gupta said he considered it a good film and credited Moore with drawing greater attention to the subject. “I think it strikes at the irrefutable fact—it’s broken. We get it,” he said.

Gupta nevertheless expressed concern about the documentary’s treatment of universal health care in other developed countries, including Canada and France. He said the film could leave viewers with the impression that care in those nations costs nothing. Although patients may not be charged when visiting a doctor, Gupta noted, the system is financed through high taxes—something he worried audiences might not understand.

Moore countered that Americans already spend more through insurance premiums, deductibles and copayments. He said the U.S. system is designed around making a profit.

Moore then asked whether Gupta found the existing arrangement burdensome, since doctors must obtain authorization from insurance companies before carrying out certain procedures.

“It’s a shameful system, especially when I’m dealing with some of my patients,” Gupta replied.

At the same time, Gupta questioned what he viewed as Moore’s proposed answer: entrusting health care to the Bush administration. Moore had strongly attacked that administration in the past, particularly in his documentary “Fahrenheit 9/11.”

“The government actually used to do things right,” Moore responded. “The problem is who we put in power.”

Moore, a firm opponent of the Iraq war, said the federal government should change its priorities. He had taken that position years before doubts about the war’s success became widespread in Washington.

Near the end of the exchange, Moore said he regretted that so much of the program had been spent trying to correct Gupta’s facts rather than discussing the larger issue—the troubled U.S. health-care system.

Video was available showing Moore and Gupta presenting their arguments, and the original article included an option to email it to a friend.

outputs.L4:
Filmmaker Michael Moore and CNN chief medical correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta engaged in a spirited debate over the facts and arguments presented in Moore’s documentary *Sicko*. The film criticizes the American health-care system and contrasts it with universal-care programs in countries including Canada, France, and the United Kingdom. Moore argued that the United States spends far more on health care than other industrialized nations while still leaving millions of people uninsured or vulnerable to denied claims, high deductibles, and overwhelming medical bills.

Gupta agreed that the American system has serious problems but challenged the way Moore presented some of his evidence. He questioned particular figures concerning per-person health-care spending, taxation, waiting times, and the performance of foreign systems. Gupta also suggested that the documentary selectively emphasized favorable examples from universal-care countries while giving less attention to their shortcomings, such as delays for some nonemergency procedures and the higher taxes used to finance public coverage.

Moore strongly rejected the accusation that he had distorted the facts. He defended the documentary’s statistics and said that its broader conclusions were supported by respected international and governmental sources. In his view, disputes over individual numbers should not obscure the film’s central point: Americans pay more for health care than people in comparable countries but do not receive universal coverage or consistently better outcomes. He also argued that private insurers and other profit-seeking institutions create incentives to restrict treatment, deny claims, and place financial considerations ahead of patients’ needs.

The discussion highlighted a fundamental difference in emphasis. Gupta approached the issue as a medical journalist concerned with precision, context, and the risks of comparing complex national systems too simply. Moore approached it as a filmmaker and advocate seeking to expose the human consequences of a system dominated by insurance companies and profit. Their disagreement therefore concerned not only the accuracy of particular statistics but also how documentary films should present evidence and whether dramatic personal stories can fairly represent a nationwide problem.

Despite the tension, the two men found substantial common ground. Both acknowledged that the U.S. health-care system is deeply flawed, excessively expensive, and unable to provide reliable care to everyone who needs it. They also agreed that profit plays too large a role in decisions that can determine whether patients receive treatment. Gupta maintained that foreign systems should not be idealized and that reform requires an honest assessment of costs and trade-offs, while Moore insisted that universal-care countries demonstrate that health care can be treated as a public service rather than primarily as a business.

Ultimately, their debate reinforced one of *Sicko*’s major achievements: it brought health-care policy into public discussion through vivid stories and international comparisons. Even where Gupta disputed Moore’s methods or conclusions, he recognized that the documentary had drawn valuable attention to a national crisis. Both agreed that the status quo was unacceptable and that the United States needed meaningful reform to make health care more accessible, affordable, and centered on patients rather than profits.

counterfactuals.output:
# Moore, Gupta trade sharp words over health care claims in ‘Sicko’

**NEW YORK —** Filmmaker Michael Moore and CNN medical correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta faced off in a heated televised debate over the accuracy of Moore’s documentary “Sicko,” clashing over health care spending, the number of uninsured Americans and the merits of universal coverage.

Appearing on CNN’s “Larry King Live” in July 2007, Moore accused the network of distorting his film’s statistics in a fact-check reported by Gupta. Gupta defended the report, saying “Sicko” raised legitimate concerns about the U.S. health care system but presented some comparisons without enough context.

The debate quickly became personal, with Moore demanding an apology and arguing that CNN had unfairly labeled parts of the documentary inaccurate.

Gupta said his report did not dispute Moore’s central argument: The American health care system leaves millions without insurance and often creates financial and bureaucratic barriers for those who are covered. But he said some of the film’s claims about spending and foreign health systems were selective or oversimplified.

## A dispute over the numbers

Much of the exchange centered on per-person health care spending in the United States and Cuba.

Moore argued that Americans spend far more per person than Cubans while failing to achieve better outcomes across several broad measures. He also challenged CNN’s presentation of the Cuban spending figure, pointing to a discrepancy in the network’s report.

Gupta acknowledged an error associated with the figure but maintained that the larger question was whether Moore’s comparisons accounted for differences in wages, infrastructure, access and the quality of care.

The two also sparred over the number of Americans without health insurance. Moore cited the widely used estimate of roughly 45 million uninsured people at the time. Gupta said that figure required context because the uninsured population included people in a range of circumstances, including some who were temporarily without coverage.

Moore countered that such distinctions did not erase the fundamental problem: Tens of millions of people could not depend on stable health coverage, while many insured Americans still faced denied claims, high costs and limited access.

## Universal coverage takes center stage

“Sicko,” released in 2007, contrasts the largely private U.S. insurance system with government-supported systems in Canada, Britain, France and Cuba. The film portrays patients in those countries receiving care without the large bills that can confront Americans.

Moore argued that health care should be treated as a public service, similar to schools, fire departments and police protection. He said a universal system could cover everyone while reducing the administrative costs and profit incentives associated with private insurance.

Gupta said universal systems provide important protections but are not free of problems. He pointed to concerns about waiting times, government budgets and access to certain specialists or procedures.

Moore accused critics of emphasizing isolated shortcomings abroad while minimizing the delays, rationing and financial burdens that already exist in the United States. In the American system, he argued, care is often rationed according to insurance status and ability to pay.

## Agreement beneath the confrontation

Despite the combative tone, Moore and Gupta shared significant common ground.

Both said the U.S. health care system was in need of major reform. Gupta said the country’s high spending did not consistently translate into superior outcomes and acknowledged that insurers and administrative complexity could interfere with medical decisions.

Their disagreement was less about whether the system was broken than about how Moore made his case — and whether “Sicko” offered a fair portrait of health care in other countries.

The confrontation reflected a broader national debate that would intensify in the years ahead: whether the United States should expand government’s role in health care, preserve an insurance-based model or adopt some combination of the two.

For Moore, the answer was clear. The stories in “Sicko,” he argued, showed that health care driven by profit had failed too many Americans.

For Gupta, the film’s message was powerful, but its statistics and comparisons still deserved scrutiny.

The televised clash offered no final resolution. But it ensured that the questions raised by “Sicko” — who gets care, who pays for it and whether health coverage should be a right — remained at the center of the political conversation.
